To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
“the low-temperature specific heat of glasses can be understood in terms of a random-matrix theory of vibrations, and the specific heat peak is proportional to the inverse of the shear modulus”.

the low-temperature specific heat of a glass is linear in temperature because the VDOS is Gaussian distributed, and the specific heat peak is inversely proportional to the shear modulus because the Gaussian distribution is broadened by anharmonic effects.

(i) the low-temperature specific heat of glasses has a linear-in-T behaviour as a consequence of the fact that the VDOS of the solid is described by random matrix theory (RMT); (ii) the specific heat peak at Tp scales inversely with the shear modulus G; (iii) the linear-in-T specific-heat anomaly is not a result of two-level tunnellings.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the low-temperature properties (specific heat, thermal expansion, thermal conductivity, etc.) of glasses.
the low-temperature properties (specific heat) of disordered solids, such as glasses.
the low-temperature specific heat and its connection to the vibrational density-of-states of glasses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the linear-in T specific heat is a universal feature of disordered solids and it is not an artefact of tunnelling states.
the specific heat anomaly is a genuine result of the structural disorder of the glass and it is a direct consequence, at classical level, of random matrix theory.
random matrix theory is a fundamental ingredient for the understanding of the specific heat behaviour of glasses, and it provides a natural explanation of their linear-in-T specific-heat behaviour.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the linear-in-temperature specific heat anomaly of glasses can be explained by the random matrix behaviour of the vibrational density-of-states of glasses.
we have demonstrated that the linear-in-temperature specific heat anomaly of glasses is a genuine property of random solids, which is a consequence of the random matrix behaviour of the VDOS.
we have been able to link the low-temperature properties (specific heat, thermal conductivity, thermal expansion) to the vibrational properties of glasses.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the linear behaviour of the specific heats of glasses at low temperatures is a direct consequence, and hence a fingerprint, of the random matrix behaviour in glasses, and that this behaviour is a genuine classical phenomenon.
the linear-in-temperature specific heat is not a quantum phenomenon, but rather it is a direct consequence, at the classical level, of random matrix theory.
the specific heat anomaly is a consequence of disorder, and it is therefore not possible to explain it by assuming the existence of a regular lattice.
